title: Yara and the Postcards
premise: After his mother's funeral, Rosalind Dravenmoor returns to the family house to catalog its silences—drawers of unopened letters, rooms arranged to avoid certain subjects, and a lifetime of things unsaid by a parent who communicated only through duty. When the estate is scheduled for auction, he discovers a cache of unsent postcards addressed to Yara Okonkwo, the childhood friend his family erased from their history after a scandal no one will name. As buyers circle the house and relatives press him to sign quickly, Rosalind traces Yara's disappearance and realizes his own invisibility was inherited—a survival strategy taught, not chosen. The novel ends at the auction itself, where Rosalind publicly asks the question the family arranged itself around for forty years, forfeits his inheritance claim, and leaves with Yara's surviving sister carrying the postcards home.
about_author: Gideon Okafor is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloging unclaimed estates in Lagos and London before turning to fiction. His work examines what families preserve, discard, and deliberately lose.

chapters.title: The Inventory Begins
chapters.summary: Rosalind, POV, arrives at the shuttered family house three days after the funeral and begins a written inventory of everything his mother never said. The emotional beat is numb precision—grief managed as clerical work.

chapters.title: Rooms That Face Away
chapters.summary: Rosalind notices the house's architecture of avoidance: a sealed sitting room, portraits turned inward. Flashback to childhood rules about which doors stayed closed. Beat: unease beneath order.

chapters.title: The Auction Notice
chapters.summary: A solicitor's letter sets the sale date—six weeks. Cousin Edmund calls urging a quick signature. Rosalind stalls, telling himself it's about the inventory. Beat: first resistance to the family script.

chapters.title: What the Drawers Kept
chapters.summary: Sorting a writing desk, Rosalind finds a bundle of unsent postcards, all addressed to 'Yara Okonkwo,' spanning decades, each one blank on the back. Beat: the first crack in the silence.

chapters.title: Yara
chapters.summary: A memory chapter: eight-year-old Rosalind and Yara by the river behind the house, an intimacy the adults tolerated then forbade. POV shifts briefly into child-logic. Beat: warmth that predates the silence.

chapters.title: The Word No One Uses
chapters.summary: Rosalind questions Aunt Margery, who deflects with recipes and weather but lets slip that Yara's family 'left under circumstances.' Beat: the family's choreography of not-knowing becomes visible.

chapters.title: Postcard, 1974
chapters.summary: Rosalind studies the earliest postcard—a seaside town—and matches it to a train timetable in his father's papers. Someone meant to go. Beat: discovery that the silence had a near-miss.

chapters.title: Edmund's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Edmund visits, appraising furniture aloud, calculating shares. He warns Rosalind against 'digging up sentiment' before the sale. Beat: duty presented as love, pressure disguised as care.

chapters.title: The Registry Office
chapters.summary: Rosalind searches public records: the Okonkwo family moved abruptly in 1975; Yara would be his age now. A forwarding address dead-ends. Beat: hope sharpened by obstruction.

chapters.title: Mother's Handwriting
chapters.summary: Examining the postcards' addresses, Rosalind recognizes his mother's hand changing over decades—young and slanted, then rigid. She wrote them all. Beat: the silent parent becomes the central mystery.

chapters.title: The Sealed Room Opened
chapters.summary: Rosalind breaks the lock on the forbidden sitting room and finds it preserved like a shrine: two teacups, a photograph of two children by the river. Beat: awe and violation entwined.

chapters.title: Margery Breaks Slightly
chapters.summary: Confronted with the room, Aunt Margery admits there was a friendship, insists it ended 'for everyone's good,' and begs him to let the house sell clean. Beat: loyalty versus truth, both grieving.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Remembers
chapters.summary: An elderly neighbor, Mrs. Halloway, recalls the Okonkwos: a father accused of theft at the mill, driven out without trial; Yara's family never defended themselves. Beat: the scandal reframed as injustice.

chapters.title: Postcards, Interrupted
chapters.summary: Rosalind finds a gap in the postcards—1976 to 1989—and understands his mother stopped writing when her own marriage began. Beat: complicity inherited across generations.

chapters.title: The Buyer from the City
chapters.summary: A property developer tours the house, planning demolition for flats. Rosalind watches the rooms valued as square footage. Beat: external deadline made visceral—the past has weeks to live.

chapters.title: Rosalind's Own Silence
chapters.summary: A quiet interior chapter: Rosalind admits he built his life on the same technique—unanswered letters, a partner left without explanation. Beat: the theme turns inward; he is his mother's heir in more than property.

chapters.title: The Letter He Never Sent
chapters.summary: Rosalind drafts and discards a message to his estranged partner, Daniel, mirroring the blank postcards. Beat: recognition of pattern; self-indictment.

chapters.title: Mill Records
chapters.summary: In county archives, Rosalind finds the 1975 theft allegation against Yara's father—and evidence suggesting the real thief was Rosalind's grandfather. Beat: the founding lie surfaces.

chapters.title: What Grandfather Arranged
chapters.summary: Rosalind pieces together how the family's wealth, reputation, even the house itself were built on the accusation. The whole family 'arranged itself around' protecting this. Beat: dread of inheritance.

chapters.title: Edmund Learns What Rosalind Knows
chapters.summary: Rosalind tests Edmund with a hint of the archive findings; Edmund goes cold and threatens legal consequences for 'defaming the dead.' Beat: open conflict begins.

chapters.title: The Sister in Leeds
chapters.summary: Through a parish newsletter, Rosalind locates Adaeze, Yara's younger sister, now a retired teacher in Leeds. He writes—then, breaking his own pattern, telephones. Beat: courage as action, not intention.

chapters.title: Adaeze
chapters.summary: POV shift to Adaeze: she remembers everything, including Yara waiting by the river for a friend who stopped coming. She agrees to meet—but warns that Yara 'doesn't talk about that house.' Beat: guarded hope.

chapters.title: The Meeting in Leeds
chapters.summary: Rosalind meets Adaeze; she shows him Yara's side of the archive: returned gifts, a kept river stone, a lifetime of watching the road. Beat: grief mirrored across the divide.

chapters.title: Where Yara Is
chapters.summary: Adaeze reveals Yara lives nearby, works with restored books, and knows the house is for sale—has known for months. Beat: proximity and terror; the meeting is possible and impossible.

chapters.title: The Question Drafted
chapters.summary: Rosalind writes out the question he must ask—why the family chose silence, and whether Yara can forgive what forgiveness cannot reach. Beat: the moral center articulated.

chapters.title: Edmund's Offer
chapters.summary: Edmund offers Rosalind a larger share if he signs immediately and hands over 'any papers causing trouble.' The bribe makes the stakes explicit. Beat: temptation priced in silver.

chapters.title: Mother's Last Postcard
chapters.summary: At the bottom of the bundle, one postcard differs: written, dated the week before her death, addressed to Yara, stamped but never posted. It says only: 'I should have come.' Beat: devastating near-redemption.

chapters.title: The River in Winter
chapters.summary: Rosalind walks the frozen riverbank where the children played, holding the stone Adaeze gave him. He decides he will not sign. Beat: resolve crystallizing in cold air.

chapters.title: Family Council
chapters.summary: Relatives convene to force the signature; Margery pleads, Edmund threatens, an uncle invokes the father's memory. Rosalind stays silent through the whole meeting—then stands and leaves. Beat: the silent heir refuses the role.

chapters.title: Restored Books
chapters.summary: Rosalind visits the book restoration workshop where Yara works, watches her through glass mending a broken spine, and cannot yet enter. Beat: suspended between fear and approach.

chapters.title: First Words in Forty Years
chapters.summary: Yara approaches him first: 'You have her chin.' A brief, raw conversation—she neither welcomes nor dismisses him. Beat: contact made; nothing resolved.

chapters.title: What Yara Knows
chapters.summary: Over tea, Yara tells her version: the accusation, the exile, the years of watching the house lights. She asks the question back: why did Rosalind stay away too? Beat: the mirror turned on him.

chapters.title: Confession at the River Stone
chapters.summary: Rosalind admits his own complicity—his silence, Daniel, the letters unsent. Yara listens without absolution but without contempt. Beat: honesty offered as the only currency he has.

chapters.title: The Auction Looms
chapters.summary: Five days remain. Edmund files to proceed without Rosalind's signature, claiming power of attorney via a document Rosalind may have signed unknowingly. Beat: legal trap closing.

chapters.title: The Solicitor's Loophole
chapters.summary: Rosalind's own solicitor finds the power-of-attorney clause is void—but contesting it publicly means airing the estate's secrets in open court or at the sale. Beat: truth and loss bound together.

chapters.title: The Night Before
chapters.summary: Rosalind spends the night in the sealed room, reading every postcard in order, then writes one of his own—to Yara, filled in completely. Beat: the inheritance transformed into voice.

chapters.title: The Auction
chapters.summary: Climax: at the sale, before bidding opens, Rosalind takes the floor and reads the grandfather's theft record aloud, then asks the family's forbidden question publicly. The room fractures; Edmund storms out; the developer withdraws amid scandal. Beat: the silence broken at maximum cost.

chapters.title: What the House Sold For
chapters.summary: Aftermath: the house sells at a fraction of its price to a local trust; Rosalind signs away his share, keeping only the postcards and the sealed room's contents. Family ties sever cleanly. Beat: loss accepted as payment for truth.

chapters.title: Delivered at Last
chapters.summary: Rosalind and Adaeze deliver the mother's final postcard to Yara together. Yara reads it alone, then places it beside the river stone. No reconciliation scene—just acknowledgment. Beat: quiet, earned grace.

chapters.title: The Letter to Daniel
chapters.summary: Resolution: on the train south, Rosalind writes to Daniel—not asking to return, but finally explaining. He mails it at the station, visible, witnessed. Beat: the cycle of silence ends in him; identity reclaimed.
